projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Ralph Edward Jarratt was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: My name is Dionna Harris and we are here with Jazmene Weatherspoon and Valerie is also in our group but she could not be here today and we are interviewing Ralph Jarrett. Today's date is October 15th 2005 and we are in New Carlise, Ohio. The interviewee's birthday is August the 4th, 1920. His war, err the war he served in his branch of service, he served in World War II and Vietnam War, he was a Colonel and he served in England, Germany, France, and Saigon, Vietnam. OK, first question: Why did you join the service?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: Well because uh they were calling everyone so I wanted to fly, if possible so I jumped in right away and was accepted as in at that time they called us uh air force cadets, or um yeah that's right air force cadets. So uh I passed all the uh written we had written tests we had to do then we had physicals that they gave us and I passed all those so then I was re was recalled into, uh to uh a base and that was in Lockland air force base in San Antonio, Texas and this is when where we did all of our pre military and uh also we did a lot of marching and uh we went to school, that was the school we went to and we had to pass the school uh what had came when it was primarily manners, manners and uh oh uh I can't tell ya I can't think as fast as I talk and but anyways uh we had many many subjects that we had to cover and that was for a period of about six weeks six six months, six months 'cuse me six months. So that is primarily why I joined it because I knew I'd be called anyway.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Okay. What was your job or assignment?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: It uh, well my time was to go to school, is what it was, and uh as I say that went on for approximately six months as I recalled. My memory's a little uh shaky, but it was around six months I went to school, and then during that time we were sent to another base and this had airplanes, small trainers, just two seaters. It was an open cockpit, so uh this is where we started are flight training and we had civilian instructors there at that time and as we progressed on through that was about uh I'd say that had to be at least six times three, had to be about eighteen, eighteen months. Eighteen months, similar to that. Then when we graduated we were sent to all different places with all different airplanes and at that time the war in uh Europe was getting quite uh fierce. So what they needed was airplanes to haul paratroopers, and the paratroopers would jump out of the plane with their chutes and uh then start, start fighting. So uh then they'd, they'd received some gliders and the gliders would hold about twelve men I guess, something like that and then when we'd got to the area where they were supposed to land, we'd they'd cut themselves off from the plane, they're just a big tow rope to pull the planes so and they would disconnect themselves and uh we had navigators on board so we could signal them when to cut off from our planes and because they would be near their landing area where they was supposed to land, which was usually in very typical just fields, that's what it was just desert fields. Now, you want to shut it off for a minute and ask me what else you wanted so I can uh get my brain to working here. [Pause in interview]

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: Yes, uh...in one nation we were flying so low, we were at 500 ft. above the Turbine because of...uh...there trip was to jumbo out and be close enough to the ground so we wouldn't get shot at. We was always being shot at and they would jump out of the plane and then...there ship would be opened above 500 ft. within free fall until they were opened and then they would land on the ground with their ammunition and what ever they needed, now they lost gliders ...I think about 12 men had equipment, and we got to the landing spot with gliders and they would run whatever they could and try and find some field we thought they landed so about 12 men with equipment....our other mission was to ....Oh and gasoline. and to go back to England, then after we dropped off our cargo usually their were army trucks their to pick up whatever we had, then the uh....they would usually have waters with people on board who were injured and shot and were still alive and we would fly back to hospitals so uh...that's it.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: How did you stay in touch with your family?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: Just by letters, just by letters.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Ok, what was the food like?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: Food, well if you liked cold pancakes, and things like that...it wasn't to bad, but, it was much better in England they had cooks there and a good kitchen, big kitchen, and we wasn't gone more than a day. A few times we were gone longer. But it was usually just a day, completes the mission and picked up wounded if there were any and go back to the base.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Was there any pressure or stress?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: Uh...I don't think so because we all helped one another keep up our spirits, you knot, and of course once your flying and your goin into combat, you become some what excited and your ready to go! Because you know its there and you have to do it so you become very excited not overly excited, but so you can complete you mission. Huh...It wasn't too bad...Brussels sprouts, we had a good time. It seem like we had those everyday, morning , noon, and night, so huh...one of our commanders said if you happen to at smart and buy some groceries in Germany, and go down, I hope its going to be in England so you can tear up the huh...the huh...excuse me what did I say patches were? Do you remember?

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Uh...I don't know.

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: Sorry, could you run that, but again?

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: You said something about Brussels sprouts?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: Ok, yea, He said if you don't fill up on Brussels sprouts then...you uh....we had those all the time.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: How did people entertain their selves?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: Oh, we would play a lot of cards, when we knew we were going to fly for a couple of days, we would go into some of the British towns and uh...just go in with our uniforms on, and try to stay out if trouble.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Ok, Were there entertainers?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: Well I remember...uh...oh uh...Let me gather my thoughts straight here...There was an orchestra, a band, then we would have pretty girls, they made a big applause. So uh...Then there was 3 or 4 others I can't think of right now.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: What were some of the pranks that you or the others would pull?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: Uh...

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Do you remember any?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: No, I really can't think of any.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Ok, well that's ok. Do you recall the day your service ended?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: Yes, I recall the day it ended. Do you want the date?

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Yes if you remember. You don't have to look for it.

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: Ok. I don't remember with out the date.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: That's ok.

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: I think it was about in the mid 1950's.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Did you work or go back to school?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: I started back to school....I was also working when I enlisted...I was a police officer on the Denver police department. I enlisted in medical. It was about in mid 1950's I can recall.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Did you join a veteran's organization?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: No, because I had a Family at that time and uh... I went back to my first job.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Do you attend any reunions?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: Yes. I just attended one uh...a year ago. It's usually in the spring, but I can no longer walk so I haven't attended one since last year.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: How does your services and your experiences affect your life?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: Well, the uh...to see our family you could write letters and they would send a picture and I would send a picture, in our uniform, or in the air plane, or next to the air plane.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Did you keep a diary?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: No, no diary, we would send our papers to ...can you shut that off for a minute.

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: We would actually go to the commanding at the air university in Maxwell Air Force Base. I think that help me go up to the land, it was promoted to Cornell, it was a good school. I went to many other schools, I went to the pilot instructor school in Alabama, and I went to air police officer school in Florida. Those schools helped out a lot. Now what I wanted to say about Libya is that we had an officer that I admired very much who was a commander in Libya and I had just arrived there when...huh... are so called Cornell ....can you shut that off .

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: You don't want it to be on here?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: No

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: What were you saying about James?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: James, Cornel...I'm gonna get that messed up. Cornel James was our commander at the air base and I had just arrived there and uh...then what we heard was he was down at the base keeping Libyans from comin' in the base because they were going to try to take over the base. So uh...he went out there and this so called cornel was heading the traits attempting to take over the air base and there was this pistol and on his hips. So uh...Cornel James told him to take his hands off of that gun or he would blow it out of his hands. So Cornel James was a black cornel and he was about 6'3", tall man, and nobody ever messed with him because he was very (You need to cut it off very soon?) 'cause he was just a very, very uh...can't get the word...he was very, very...let me see...he loved air force and he really helped out anybody in the air force, and he had a...can't think of the word...he was very...had a 100% legatee to the air force, and so he wouldn't let them in. So uh...he kept the Libyans off of base because the air force had a lot of air craft so uh...

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Why did you pick the service branch you joined?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: Because it was flying and I wanted to fly.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Do you remember your instructors?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: I wish I did.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Ok. Was there something special you did for good luck?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: No, I just prayed the good Lord would take care of me.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: What did you think of officers of fellow soldiers?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: They were very uh...very original to the service...very much. I don't think we had any trouble. Everybody was ready to go, and went.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Did you make any close friendships while in the service?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: Oh yea...you can't help it because there's probably 10 or 15 of you sleeping in the same barracks and you were eating and sleeping together. So uh...being a farm boy, I really didn't have any trouble. It was pretty good.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Excuse the interruptions. So uh...etc...right here. Uh...I wish we could...

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Did you feel pressured or stress?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: We only flew 500 ft above the ground so, no. The wind was our enemy.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Did your military experience influence you about military at all?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: Yes, I thought a lot about it.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Did you want to continue about your record?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: It was hand shakes and greetings. I had quite a few telephone calls.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Is there anything else that you would to add to this interview?

sp.speaker: Ralph Edward Jarratt
sp.p: No, that's pretty much it.

sp.speaker: Dionna Harris
sp.p: Well, thank you for your time and we'll keep in touch.
